name: Song of Songs
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (Old Greek) through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Fragments of four Song of Songs manuscripts were found at Qumran (4QCant-a, -b, -c and 6QCant); where the variants cited are not verified individually they are described as “some ancient witnesses.” The Hebrew text has no speaker labels, but its grammar (masculine and feminine forms, singular and plural) usually shows who is speaking; the speakers are identified only in the footnotes (“She,” “He,” “The friends,” the “daughters of Jerusalem”), and no headings have been added. Plants, spices, and places are explained at their first appearance. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; English 6:13 is Hebrew 7:1, so Hebrew 7:2–14 is English 7:1–13.

verses.text: The Song of Songs,{a} which is Solomon’s.{b}

Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,{c}
for your love{d} is better than wine.

Draw me after you; let us run!
The king has brought me into his chambers.
We will rejoice and delight in you;{e}
we will praise your love more than wine.
How right they are to love you!

Black am I, and lovely,
you daughters of Jerusalem,
dark as the tents of Kedar,{f}
as the hangings of Solomon.

Do not look down on me for being dark,
for the sun has burned me.
My brothers were furious with me;
they put me in charge of the vineyards,
but my own vineyard I neglected.

Tell me, my beloved,
where you pasture your flock,
where you rest them at noon?
Why should I wander like a veiled woman{g}
among your friends’ flocks?

If you do not know, loveliest of women,
go out in the footprints of the sheep
and feed your kids
near the tents of the shepherds.{h}

To a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots
I compare you, my darling.{i}

Lovely are your cheeks between the earrings,
your neck among the beads.

Earrings of gold we will make for you,
dotted with silver.{j}

While the king lay on his couch,
my nard{k} spread out its scent.

My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh{l}
that lies all night between my breasts.

My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms{m}
in the vineyards of En-gedi.{n}

Look at you, my darling, so beautiful,
so beautiful! Your eyes are doves.{o}

How handsome you are, my beloved, how delightful!{p}
Our couch is green and leafy;

the beams of our house are cedars,
our rafters are junipers.{q}

notes.text: A Hebrew way of saying “the finest song.”
Or “for Solomon” or “about Solomon.” The name Shelomoh is connected with shalom, “peace.”
She speaks in verses 2–4, turning from “him” to “you.” The Hebrew has no speaker labels; here and below they are inferred from the grammar.
Hebrew dodim, “lovemaking” or “caresses”; also in verse 4. The Septuagint, reading the same letters differently, has “your breasts.”
The plural “we” may be the young women of verse 3 or the friends; “you” is masculine.
Kedar, a tribe of the Syrian–Arabian desert, whose name may mean “dark”; their tents were woven of black goat hair.
Perhaps veiled as a prostitute (compare Genesis 38:14–15); some ancient witnesses read “one who wanders.”
He replies in verse 8, or perhaps the friends.
He speaks in verses 9–11. Hebrew ra‘yati, “my companion,” his usual word for her in the Song. A mare loosed among chariot stallions was a famous image of distraction.
The “we” here may be his companions or the friends.
She speaks in verses 12–14. Nard, or spikenard, a costly perfume from a plant of the Himalayas.
Myrrh, a fragrant resin from trees of Arabia and East Africa, worn in a small pouch.
Henna, a shrub with fragrant clusters of white flowers, also used for dye.
En-gedi, “spring of the young goat,” an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea.
He speaks.
She speaks in verses 16–17; some divide verse 17 between them.
Or “firs” or “cypresses”; the exact tree is uncertain.

verses.text:
I am a crocus{a} of Sharon,{b}
a lily of the valleys.

As a lily among the brambles,
so is my darling among the girls.{c}

Like an apple tree{d} among the trees of the forest,
so is my beloved among the young men.{e}
In his shade I delight to sit,
and his fruit is sweet to my taste.

He has brought me to the house of wine,
and his banner over me is love.

Revive me with raisin cakes,
refresh me with apples,
for I am faint with love.

His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles, by the wild does:
do not rouse, do not wake love
until it wishes!{f}

Hark! My beloved!
See, he is coming,
springing across the mountains,
bounding over the hills.

My beloved is like a gazelle
or a fawn of the deer.
There he is, standing outside our wall,
looking in at the windows,
glancing through the latticework.

My beloved answers me and says,
“Up, my darling,
my beautiful one, come away,

for look, the winter is past;
the rain has ended and gone.

Blossoms appear in the land,
the season of singing{g} has come,
and the cooing of the turtledove
is heard in our land.

The fig tree ripens its early figs,
and the vines in bloom give off fragrance.
Arise, my darling,
my beautiful one, and come away.

My dove in the clefts of the rock,
in the hiding places of the cliff,
show me your form,
let your voice be heard,
for sweet is the sound of you
and lovely the sight of you.”

Seize the foxes for us,{h}
those little foxes
that spoil the vineyards
now that our vines are blossoming.

My beloved is mine and I am his;
he grazes among the lilies.

Until the day breathes
and the shadows slip away,
come back, my beloved, like a gazelle
or a fawn of the deer
on the cleft mountains.{i}

notes.text: She speaks. The flower is uncertain: crocus, narcissus, or some other meadow flower; the Septuagint has “a flower of the plain.”
Sharon, the coastal plain south of Mount Carmel, known for its pastures and wildflowers; the name means “plain.”
He speaks.
Hebrew tappuach, perhaps the apple, apricot, or quince.
She speaks in verses 3–17.

A wordplay: tsevaoth, “gazelles,” and ’ayloth hassadeh, “does of the field,” sound like the divine titles “Yahweh of hosts” and “God Almighty” (El Shaddai), as though she swears by them in a veiled way. The Septuagint reads “by the powers and by the virtues of the field.” The refrain returns in 3:5 and 8:4.
Or “pruning,” as in the Septuagint; Hebrew zamir can mean either.
The speaker of verse 15 is uncertain; perhaps she quotes a song, or her brothers speak (compare 1:6).
Or “the mountains of Bether,” an unknown place, or “the mountains of spices” (compare 8:14). The Septuagint has “the mountains of the ravines.”

verses.text:
“I will rise now and go around the city,
through the streets and the squares;
I will seek the one my soul loves.”
I sought him but did not find him.

The watchmen came upon me,
those who patrol the city.
“The one my soul loves: have you seen him?”

I had barely left them
when I met the man I love.
I grabbed him and refused to release him
until I brought him to my mother’s home,
to the chamber of the woman who bore me.

I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles, by the wild does:
do not rouse, do not wake love
until it wishes!

all of them gripping swords,
trained in battle,
each with his sword at his thigh
against the terrors of the night.

King Solomon made himself a carriage{d}
of wood from Lebanon.{e}

Its posts he made of silver,
its back of gold,
its seat of purple wool,
its interior inlaid with love{f}
by the daughters of Jerusalem.

Come out, women of Zion,
and look at King Solomon
in the crown his mother set on him
at his wedding,
on the day his heart was glad.

notes.text: She speaks in verses 1–5. Literally “in the nights.”
The speaker of verses 6–11 is unstated: perhaps the friends or a narrator. “Who is this” is feminine in Hebrew, referring to the litter or to the bride.
Frankincense, a white resin from trees of southern Arabia and Somalia, burned as incense.
Hebrew ’appiryon, found only here, perhaps a loanword from Persian or Greek for a palanquin or sedan chair.
Lebanon, “white,” from its snowcapped peaks, famous for its cedars.
Or “inlaid with leather,” by a related Semitic word; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes
come up from the washing,
every one of them bearing twins,
and none among them bereaved.

A scarlet ribbon, those lips of yours,
and lovely is your mouth.
Like a half of pomegranate
is your temple behind your veil.

Your neck is like the tower of David,
built in courses,{c}
with a thousand shields hung on it,
all the round shields of warriors.

Your breasts are two fawns,
a gazelle’s twins,
grazing among the lilies.

Until the day breathes
and the shadows slip away,
I will go to the mountain of myrrh
and to the hill of frankincense.

You are beautiful through and through, my darling;
there is no flaw in you.

How fine is your love, my sister, my bride!
How much better your love than wine,
and the scent of your oils than any spice!

A garden locked up is my sister, my bride,
a spring{g} locked up, a fountain sealed.

Your shoots are an orchard{h} of pomegranates
with choicest fruits,
henna with nard,

You are a fountain in the gardens,
a well of living water,
streams flowing down from Lebanon.

notes.text: He speaks in verses 1–15.
Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan, known for its pastures; the name may mean “heap of witness” (compare Genesis 31:47–48).
Hebrew talpiyyoth, found only here; the meaning is uncertain: perhaps “in courses of stone,” “for weapons,” or “as a landmark.”
The Septuagint reads “Come from Lebanon, my bride.” The Hebrew “with me” may be read with a slight change of vowels as “come.”
Amana, a peak in the Anti-Lebanon range; Senir, the Amorite name for Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9), or a nearby peak. Hermon, the highest mountain of the region, about 9,200 feet (2,814 meters).
“Sister” was a term of endearment for a beloved or bride in ancient Near Eastern love poetry; it does not imply kinship.
Hebrew gal, perhaps “pool” or “spring”; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read gan, “garden,” repeating the first line.
Hebrew pardes, “park” or “orchard” (compare Ecclesiastes 2:5).
Saffron, the dried stigmas of the crocus, used as a spice and dye.
Calamus, a fragrant reed or cane imported from the east (compare Exodus 30:23).
Aloes here means eaglewood, a fragrant Asian wood, not the medicinal aloe plant.
She speaks in verse 16.

verses.text:
My beloved thrust his hand through the opening,{d}
and my insides stirred for him.

I got up to open to my beloved,
and my hands dripped with myrrh,
my fingers with liquid myrrh,
on the handles of the bolt.

I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem:
if you find my beloved,
what will you tell him?
That I am faint with love!

What makes your beloved better than any other,{f}
most beautiful of women?
What makes your beloved better than any other,
that you put us under oath like this?

My beloved is dazzling and ruddy,{g}
one who stands out among ten thousand.

His eyes are doves
by the water brooks,
washed in milk,
sitting in their settings.{i}

His cheeks are like beds of spice,
towers of perfumes.{j}
His lips are lilies
dripping liquid myrrh.

His legs are marble columns
resting on golden bases.
He looks as majestic as Lebanon,
as stately as cedar trees.

His mouth is utter sweetness;
he is wholly desirable.
Such is my lover, such is my friend,
women of Jerusalem.

notes.text: He speaks in the first four lines.
Or “drink deep of love.” The speaker of these two lines is uncertain: the friends, a narrator, or he himself.
She speaks in verses 2–8, recounting a dream-like night; he speaks in verse 2 and she answers in verse 3.
Literally “through the hole,” probably the keyhole or latch opening of the door.
Or “when he turned away”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The daughters of Jerusalem speak in verse 9.
She answers in verses 10–16. Hebrew tsach, “radiant” or “shining.”
Hebrew taltallim, found only here, perhaps “like palm fronds” or “curly.”
Or “sitting by brimming pools”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
So the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “pouring out perfumes,” with a change of vowels.
Tarshish, a distant port, perhaps in Spain; here probably a gemstone named for it, such as beryl or topaz.
Literally “sapphires”; the ancient stone of that name was probably lapis lazuli.

verses.text:
Where did your beloved go,{a}
loveliest among women?
In what direction did your beloved turn,
that we may seek him along with you?

My beloved has gone down to his garden,{b}
to the beds of spice,
to graze in the gardens
and to gather lilies.

I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine;
he grazes among the lilies.

Turn your eyes away from me,
for they overwhelm me.
Your hair is a flock of goats
streaming down from Gilead.

Your teeth are a flock of ewes
come up from the washing,
every one of them bearing twins,
and none among them bereaved.

Like a half of pomegranate
is your temple behind your veil.

There may be sixty queens
and eighty concubines,
and young women past counting,

but my dove, my flawless one, is matchless,
her mother’s only daughter,
the pride of the woman who bore her.
Young women saw her and declared her happy;
queens and concubines sang her praise:

“Who is she, gazing out like the morning,
lovely as the moon,{e}
radiant as the sun,
formidable as an army with banners?”

I went down to the nut grove{f}
to see the new growth of the valley,
to see whether the vine had budded
and the pomegranates were in bloom.

Before I knew it, my desire set me
among the chariots of my noble people.{g}

notes.text: The daughters of Jerusalem speak in verse 1.
She speaks in verses 2–3.
He speaks in verses 4–10. Tirzah, “she is pleasing,” was a beautiful city and early royal capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 14:17; 16:23); the Septuagint translates the name as “Pleasure.”
Or “as the starry hosts”; the Hebrew nidgaloth is uncertain. Also in verse 10.
The poetic words here are levanah, “the white one,” for the moon, and chammah, “the hot one,” for the sun.
The speaker of verses 11–12 is uncertain, probably she, possibly he.
Or “among the chariots of Amminadib,” as a name, “my kinsman is noble”; the Septuagint has “the chariots of Aminadab.” The Hebrew of this verse is among the most obscure in the book.

In Hebrew this verse is 7:1, and 7:1–13 below are Hebrew 7:2–14. The friends call to her in the first two lines; she, or he, answers in the last two. Shulammite may mean “woman of Shulem” (perhaps Shunem, as in the Septuagint), or be a feminine form linked with Solomon and shalom, “the peaceful one.”
Or “the dance of Mahanaim,” a town east of the Jordan whose name means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2).

verses.text:
Your navel is a round goblet
that never runs short of spiced wine.
Your waist is a mound of wheat
hedged about with lilies.

Your two breasts are like two fawns,
twins of a gazelle.

How lovely you are, how delightful,
love, among all delights!{g}

This stature of yours is like a palm tree,
and your breasts are its clusters.

I said, “I will climb the palm tree;
I will take hold of its fruit stalks.”
May your breasts be like clusters of the vine,
the scent of your breath like apples,

I am my beloved’s,
and his desire is for me.

Let us go early to the vineyards
to see whether the vine has budded,
whether its blossoms have opened
and the pomegranates are in flower.
There I will give you my love.

The mandrakes{k} breathe out their scent,
and at our doors are all the finest fruits,
fresh ones and stored ones,
that I have laid up for you, my beloved.

notes.text: He speaks in verses 1–9a, or the friends in verses 1–5. English 7:1–13 is Hebrew 7:2–14.
Literally “daughter of a noble” or “prince’s daughter.”
Heshbon, “reckoning,” a city east of the Jordan, in what is now Jordan, known for its reservoirs.
Bath-rabbim, “daughter of many,” probably the name of a city gate.
Carmel, “garden land” or “orchard,” the wooded ridge rising above the Mediterranean near modern Haifa.
Purple dye, from the murex shell, was the costliest color in the ancient world.
Or “O loved one, daughter of delights,” following some ancient witnesses with a different division of the Hebrew letters.
She takes up his words in the last two lines and speaks in verses 10–13.
So the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “over my lips and teeth.”
Or “in the villages”; Hebrew kefarim can mean either.
Mandrakes, a plant with a fragrant yellow fruit, thought to stir love and fertility (compare Genesis 30:14–16).

verses.text:
Oh, that you were like my own brother,{a}
one suckled at my mother’s breast!
Then if I met you outside, I could kiss you,
and no one would think less of me.

I would guide you and bring you
to my mother’s home, where she would instruct me.{b}
I would give you spiced wine to drink,
the nectar of my pomegranates.

His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

Many waters cannot put out love,
and rivers will not sweep it away.
If someone offered all the wealth of his house for love,
he would be utterly scorned.

We have a little sister,{h}
and she has no breasts yet.
What shall we do for our sister
on the day she is spoken for?

If she is a wall,
we will build on her a parapet of silver;
but if she is a door,
we will board her up with planks of cedar.

My vineyard, my very own, is mine to give.
The twenty-five pounds are yours, Solomon,
and five pounds{m} for those who tend its fruit.

Hurry away, my beloved,{o}
and be like a gazelle
or a fawn of the deer
on the mountains of spices.

notes.text: She speaks in verses 1–4.
Or, with the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses, “into the room of the one who conceived me” (compare 3:4).
The refrain of 2:7 and 3:5, here without the oath by gazelles and does, and phrased as a question.
The friends speak in the first two lines.
She speaks in verses 5b–7. In the Hebrew, “you” in this verse is masculine. The Septuagint begins this verse “Who is this that comes up all white.”
Or “jealousy,” Hebrew qin’ah, the intense ardor of love.

Hebrew shalhevetyah. The ending -yah may be the short form of the divine name, “a flame of Yahweh,” or it may simply intensify the word, “a mighty flame,” as Hebrew sometimes uses divine names for a superlative. This is the only possible mention of God in the Song.
Her brothers speak in verses 8–9 (compare 1:6).
She speaks in verses 10–12.
Hebrew shalom, perhaps a wordplay on Solomon (Shelomoh) and the Shulammite (6:13).
Baal-hamon, “owner of abundance” or “lord of a multitude,” an unknown place; the name may be symbolic.
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 11.5 kilograms.
Hebrew “two hundred,” that is, two hundred shekels of silver, about 2.3 kilograms.
He speaks in verse 13; “you” is feminine.
She speaks in verse 14 (compare 2:17).
